content: ABCD1 is a protein responsible for the transport of fatty acids into peroxisomes. The protein encoded by the ABCD1 gene belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily. ABC transporters are specialized proteins that facilitate the movement of various molecules across both extracellular and intracellular membranes. The ABC transporter family is categorized into seven distinct subfamilies: ABC1, MDR/TAP, MRP, ALD, OABP, GCN20, and White. ABCD1 is specifically a member of the ALD subfamily, which plays a critical role in the peroxisomal import of fatty acids and/or fatty acyl-CoAs into the organelle. All known peroxisomal ABC transporters, including ABCD1, are classified as half-transporters. These half-transporters require the presence of a partner half-transporter molecule to form a functional transporter, which can either be a homodimer or a heterodimer. ABCD1 is a peroxisomal membrane protein that is believed to be involved in the transport or breakdown of very long-chain fatty acids within peroxisomes. Mutations or defects in the ABCD1 gene have been identified as the cause of adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), a demyelinating disorder of the nervous system that is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. To study the function of ABCD1, model organisms have been utilized. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Abcd1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was developed as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program, conducted at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute, is a large-scale mutagenesis initiative aimed at creating and distributing animal models of human diseases for research purposes. Both male and female mice with the ABCD1 gene deletion underwent a standardized phenotypic screening process to assess the effects of the gene's absence. A total of 24 tests were performed on these mutant mice, but no significant abnormalities were detected. Additionally, ABCD1 has been shown to interact with PEX19, a protein involved in peroxisomal biogenesis and function.
